reasoning: MSA-origin abstract noun that Palestinians use in conversation. It keeps q, and th is often kept in this register (some speakers say taqaafe or ta'aafe). Taa marbuta after ف is e.
3ala is reduced to 3a. إيد 'hand' is iid with long ii, and the article assimilates to ش. Literally 'on the left hand'; many speakers contract shimaal to shmaal.
Contracted from kull shi, with doubled l and a final short i. Common everyday Palestinian for 'everything'.
The 1st-person past of نجح contracts to nja7t. bi + il- gives bil-, and the initial hamza of imti7aan is written as a vowel.
Brand loanword used across the Levant. The first vowel is short i and the stress falls on the final ee. Palestinians use it for any instant coffee.

The 1st-person present is b + aDunn, with doubled n. I write ظ as D since urban speech has no interdentals, though some speakers say an emphatic z. آه is the Palestinian 'yes', so this means 'I think so'.

meaning_fix: valuable / of great worth (formal, e.g. advice, information)
reasoning: A formal, book-register adjective that keeps q. 'Worthy' is slightly off; it means valuable or worthwhile. In conversation a Palestinian would say ghaali, or use مهم for 'important'.
MSA-origin word used in everyday Palestinian for home heating. Taa marbuta after hamza is e by the scheme rule; some speakers say tadfiye.
Standard everyday word for 'easy', short a and sukun on ه.

romanization: yaa ghaayib 3an il-3eyn yaa ghaayib 3an il-'alb
vowelled_arabic: يَا غَايِب عَن العِين يَا غَايِب عَن القَلْب
reasoning: عين is 3een with long ee and ق in قلب is a glottal stop. The line literally addresses the absent one, but it corresponds to the idiom 'out of sight, out of mind'.
Palestinian 3imil 'he did/made' plus the English loan skriin shoot. The loan is spelled with و, so I write shoot.
ثانية is taanye, with ث as t and taa marbuta as e. Taa marbuta after ه is also e. The phrase is a discourse connector meaning 'and on the other hand'.
MSA-origin political term that Palestinians use daily in current discussion. Both ض are emphatic D and the colloquial plural is araaDi.
Urban Palestinian for 'my grandfather' is sidi with short vowels, like sitti for grandmother. جدي (jiddi) is also used.

يصبرك is yiSabbrak, with emphatic ص and doubled b, and the vowel drops before -ak. In يقويك the ق is a glottal stop and the stem-final ii lengthens before -k. The suffix -ak marks the masculine addressee.
Instrument-noun pattern mif3ala gives minshafe, and taa marbuta after ف is e. It is used in Palestinian speech; فوطة is also heard.
مين is miin with long ii. The ما of 'whoever' is short (ma) in connected speech.
Urban Palestinian often monophthongizes aw to oo, as in zooj 'husband'; some speakers keep zawje. Taa marbuta after ج is e. The colloquial 'my wife' is often zoojti or martti.
شلون is Iraqi/Gulf, and in Syria it is regional. A Ramallah speaker says keef.
The noun nitiije 'result' is colloquial, but the prepositional use 'as a result of' is a formal register. In conversation a Palestinian would say bisabab or 3ashaan.
ث becomes t and aw becomes oo, so thawb is toob. مطرز is muTarraz with emphatic ط and doubled r. Some speakers keep th in this heritage term.

ma + shuft 'I saw' + -u 'him' + the -sh negation suffix, which is found in Palestinian and Egyptian. Shuft (not shift) is the urban form. The vowel before -sh could also be oo, and the form could also mean 'you (pl.) didn't see'.
The standard Levantine/Palestinian word for tomato, with long oo. Taa marbuta after ر is a.
Political proper-noun term, so ق stays q, though casual speech may say 'iTaa3. Palestinian Gaza is ghazze with doubled z and final e.
Loanword kiilo with long ii, used for both 'kilogram' and 'kilo' in shops.
